cue: How do you say someone brought up exactly the painful thing?

es.text: Meter el dedo en la llaga
es.literal: to put one's finger in the wound
es.meaning: To touch deliberately on the most painful or awkward point.
es.example: Preguntó por el divorcio delante de todos: metió el dedo en la llaga.
es.exampleTranslation: He asked about the divorce in front of everyone — he went straight for the sore spot.

it.literal: to put one's finger in the wound
it.meaning: To touch deliberately on the most painful or awkward point.
it.example: Ha chiesto del divorzio davanti a tutti: ha messo il dito nella piaga.
it.exampleTranslation: He asked about the divorce in front of everyone — he went straight for the sore spot.

bridge.note: This one is identical on both sides, and unusually the identity is the lesson rather than a shortcut. Both descend from the same scene — Thomas, told the risen Christ has appeared, saying he will not believe until he puts his finger into the wound — so the phrase did not arrive in each language separately and converge by luck. It was already there, in the book both cultures read. Worth knowing that other languages did not all inherit it the same way: French twists a knife in the wound instead.

interference.es_to_it: Almost nothing to trip on. Watch only the noun: Italian piaga against Spanish llaga — both from Latin plaga, but Spanish turned the initial pl- into ll-, a regular sound change that shows up across the vocabulary (pluvia/lluvia, plenus/lleno). Learning it here makes several other words predictable.
interference.it_to_es: Same in reverse: the Italian pi- corresponds to Spanish ll- in this family of words. The construction, the article and the preposition all match, so the sound change is the only thing to carry across.
